summary_html: **Mandatory reporters** (designated professionals) must report suspected child abuse or neglect. Federal law sets the funding and policy floor (CAPTA) and mandates reporter frameworks on federal lands/facilities (VICAA).
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — federal floor for state reporting systems  
- **Victims of Child Abuse Act (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — includes federal-facility reporter duties (recodified from former 42 U.S.C. §13031)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held that Minnesota's child-abuse reporting act creates no private civil cause of action against a mandatory reporter who fails to report suspected abuse, because the legislature chose to impose only criminal penalties.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Minnesota Supreme Court statement of what a mandatory reporter owes and what happens when the duty is breached — criminal exposure, not civil liability.
key_cases.quote: The plain language of the statute indicates that the legislature chose to impose criminal, but not civil, penalties on mandatory reporters who fail to report.

key_cases.holding: The court held that Minnesota's Reporting of Maltreatment of Minors Act creates no express or implied civil cause of action for bad-faith reporting or investigation, and that the county defendants' statements were protected by a qualified privilege.
key_cases.relevance: It forecloses a civil suit against a mandated reporter even on an allegation that the report was made in bad faith.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that there is no express or implied civil cause of action under RMMA for bad faith reporting or investigating child maltreatment.

key_cases.case_name: Fosselman v. Commissioner of Human Services
key_cases.holding: The court held that maltreatment-based disqualification proceedings against mandated reporters are subject to procedural due process and that making the commissioner's reconsideration the final agency action, with no evidentiary hearing, denied relators due process.
key_cases.relevance: Mandated reporters who are found to have failed to report face disqualification, and this case establishes that they are constitutionally entitled to process before that finding sticks.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that disqualification proceedings are subject to the requirements of procedural due process.

key_cases.holding: Affirming summary judgment, the court held that the Child Abuse Reporting Act imposes no duty between a mandated reporter and the abused child that can support a negligence action, so failure to report gives rise to no civil cause of action.
key_cases.relevance: This is the original Minnesota holding that a mandated reporter's failure to report supports no private damages action — the first link in the Valtakis / Kuelbs / Becker line that Kuelbs expressly rests on.
key_cases.quote: Since CARA created the duty to report, a civil action cannot lie outside the express or clearly implied language of the statute.

key_cases.holding: Reversing the dismissal of the prosecution, the court held that Minnesota's child-abuse reporting statute is neither unconstitutionally vague nor overbroad, and that it reaches a mandated reporter whose failure to report is merely negligent rather than knowing or reckless.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court decision sustaining criminal prosecution of a mandated reporter and construing the 'knows or has reason to believe' trigger, and it is the enforcement mechanism Becker later identified as the only one the legislature provided.
key_cases.quote: Holding that the statute is not unconstitutionally vague or overbroad, we reverse and remand to the district court for further proceedings.

state_agency.name: Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families
state_agency.hotline: No statewide hotline. Call the county or Tribal child protection agency where the child lives — the directory link is on dcyf.mn.gov/individuals-and-families/report-abuse

mandatory_reporters: Designated professionals only (not universal) — Minn. Stat. § 260E.06, subd. 1; any person may voluntarily report but is not required to (§ 260E.06, subd. 2)
A professional or professional's delegate engaged in the practice of the healing arts — Minn. Stat. § 260E.06, subd. 1(a)(1)

A professional or professional's delegate engaged in social services, including employee assistance counseling and guardian ad litem and parenting time expeditor services — Minn. Stat. § 260E.06, subd. 1(a)(1) and (b)
A professional or professional's delegate engaged in hospital administration — Minn. Stat. § 260E.06, subd. 1(a)(1)
A professional or professional's delegate engaged in psychological or psychiatric treatment — Minn. Stat. § 260E.06, subd. 1(a)(1)
A professional or professional's delegate engaged in child care — Minn. Stat. § 260E.06, subd. 1(a)(1)
A professional or professional's delegate engaged in education — Minn. Stat. § 260E.06, subd. 1(a)(1)
A professional or professional's delegate engaged in correctional supervision or probation and correctional services — Minn. Stat. § 260E.06, subd. 1(a)(1)
A professional or professional's delegate engaged in law enforcement — Minn. Stat. § 260E.06, subd. 1(a)(1)
A member of the clergy who received the information while engaged in ministerial duties, except information privileged under § 595.02, subd. 1(c) — Minn. Stat. § 260E.06, subd. 1(a)(2)

An employee or supervisor of a private or public youth recreation program (including coaching staff), as to abuse by another employee or supervisor or abuse a child discloses — Minn. Stat. § 260E.055, subd. 1(d) and subd. 2

A parent, guardian, or caretaker relying on spiritual means or prayer in lieu of medical care, when the lack of medical care may cause serious danger to the child's health — Minn. Stat. § 260E.06, subd. 3

timeline_requirements.deadline: Except in a noncaregiver human trafficking assessment: immediately if sexual abuse or substantial child endangerment is alleged; within 5 calendar days for all other screened in reports
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified by statute; Minn. Stat. § 260E.20, subd. 2(b) sets the face-to-face contact deadline for the local welfare agency.
timeline_requirements.extension_grounds: Face-to-face contact on a report alleging sexual abuse or substantial child endangerment may be postponed for no more than five calendar days if the child is residing in a location confirmed to restrict contact with the alleged offender, or if the local welfare agency is pursuing a court order for the caregiver to produce the child for questioning under Minn. Stat. § 260E.22, subd. 5 (§ 260E.20, subd. 2(b)).

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified by statute; Minn. Stat. § 260E.24, subd. 1 requires the local welfare agency to conclude the assessment or investigation within 45 days.
timeline_requirements.extension_grounds: Only to complete a criminal investigation or to receive expert information requested within 45 days of receipt of the report (Minn. Stat. § 260E.24, subd. 1).
